claim: The relationship between Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent (BOLD) responses in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and increases or decreases in neural firing rate across human brain regions, especially the association cortex, remains largely unknown.
source: The relationship between Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent (BOLD) responses in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and increases or decreases in neural firing rate across human brain regions, especially the association cortex, remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge regarding BOLD-neural firing relationships in human association cortex.

claim: Animal studies have characterized Blood-Oxygenation-Level-Dependent (BOLD) fMRI activation as a correlate of local synaptic activity.
source: While animal studies have characterized Blood-Oxygenation-Level-Dependent (BOLD) fMRI activation as a correlate of local synaptic activity (Logothetis et al., 2001; Bartolo et al., 2011), the cellular mechanisms of deactivation (negative BOLD signals) remain unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to Logothetis et al., 2001 and Bartolo et al., 2011.

claim: The cellular mechanisms of deactivation (negative BOLD signals) remain unknown.
source: While animal studies have characterized Blood-Oxygenation-Level-Dependent (BOLD) fMRI activation as a correlate of local synaptic activity (Logothetis et al., 2001; Bartolo et al., 2011), the cellular mechanisms of deactivation (negative BOLD signals) remain unknown.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge regarding negative BOLD signals.

claim: fMRI deactivations have been attributed to (relative) decreases in neuronal activity.
source: Since BOLD activity relies on contrasts between (two) conditions of interest, fMRI deactivations have been attributed to various causes, that is (relative) decreases in neuronal activity (Shmuel et al., 2006; Devor et al., 2008; Boorman et al., 2010), (relative) increases in neural activity (without concomitant compensation by cerebral blood flow [CBF] increase; Schridde et al., 2008), or hemodynamic contributions ('blood stealing'; Harel et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shmuel et al., 2006; Devor et al., 2008; Boorman et al., 2010.

claim: fMRI deactivations have been attributed to (relative) increases in neural activity without concomitant compensation by cerebral blood flow increase.
source: Since BOLD activity relies on contrasts between (two) conditions of interest, fMRI deactivations have been attributed to various causes, that is (relative) decreases in neuronal activity (Shmuel et al., 2006; Devor et al., 2008; Boorman et al., 2010), (relative) increases in neural activity (without concomitant compensation by cerebral blood flow [CBF] increase; Schridde et al., 2008), or hemodynamic contributions ('blood stealing'; Harel et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schridde et al., 2008.

claim: fMRI deactivations have been attributed to hemodynamic contributions ('blood stealing').
source: Since BOLD activity relies on contrasts between (two) conditions of interest, fMRI deactivations have been attributed to various causes, that is (relative) decreases in neuronal activity (Shmuel et al., 2006; Devor et al., 2008; Boorman et al., 2010), (relative) increases in neural activity (without concomitant compensation by cerebral blood flow [CBF] increase; Schridde et al., 2008), or hemodynamic contributions ('blood stealing'; Harel et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harel et al., 2002.

claim: fMRI deactivation is associated with electrocorticographic alpha power decrease in the human visual cortex.
source: However, notwithstanding recent evidence of fMRI deactivation associated with electrocorticographic alpha power decrease in the human visual cortex (Fracasso et al., 2022), most studies have been carried out in animal models and primary sensory or motor regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fracasso et al., 2022.

claim: Most studies on BOLD deactivation have been carried out in animal models and primary sensory or motor regions.
source: However, notwithstanding recent evidence of fMRI deactivation associated with electrocorticographic alpha power decrease in the human visual cortex (Fracasso et al., 2022), most studies have been carried out in animal models and primary sensory or motor regions.
evidence: Statement about the distribution of prior research on BOLD deactivation.

claim: Two patients with refractory epilepsy (P1, P2) were implanted with hybrid macro-microelectrodes in their fusiform gyrus.
source: Specifically, two patients with refractory epilepsy (P1, P2) were implanted with hybrid macro-microelectrodes in their fusiform gyrus, a hominoid-specific cortical structure (Weiner and Zilles, 2016) that is critically involved in face recognition (Cohen et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of the experimental subjects and procedure.

claim: The fusiform gyrus is a hominoid-specific cortical structure.
source: Specifically, two patients with refractory epilepsy (P1, P2) were implanted with hybrid macro-microelectrodes in their fusiform gyrus, a hominoid-specific cortical structure (Weiner and Zilles, 2016) that is critically involved in face recognition (Cohen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiner and Zilles, 2016.

claim: The fusiform gyrus is critically involved in face recognition.
source: Specifically, two patients with refractory epilepsy (P1, P2) were implanted with hybrid macro-microelectrodes in their fusiform gyrus, a hominoid-specific cortical structure (Weiner and Zilles, 2016) that is critically involved in face recognition (Cohen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2019.

claim: Microelectrodes recording single-unit activity in P1 were located in the lateral portion of the middle fusiform gyrus (MidFG) in cytoarchitectonic area FG4.
source: While microelectrodes recording single-unit activity located in the lateral portion of P1's middle fusiform gyrus (MidFG) (i.e., in cytoarchitectonic area FG4; Lorenz et al., 2017), a region known to elicit larger BOLD activity to faces than non-face objects ('Fusiform Face Area', FFA; Kanwisher et al., 1997), in P2 they fell in the medial MidFG portion (FG3), in which lower BOLD responses to faces than objects are typically observed (Pelphrey et al., 2003; Kanwisher, 2017; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of electrode location with citation to Lorenz et al., 2017 for cytoarchitectonic area.

claim: The lateral portion of the middle fusiform gyrus (area FG4) is a region known to elicit larger BOLD activity to faces than non-face objects ('Fusiform Face Area', FFA).
source: While microelectrodes recording single-unit activity located in the lateral portion of P1's middle fusiform gyrus (MidFG) (i.e., in cytoarchitectonic area FG4; Lorenz et al., 2017), a region known to elicit larger BOLD activity to faces than non-face objects ('Fusiform Face Area', FFA; Kanwisher et al., 1997), in P2 they fell in the medial MidFG portion (FG3), in which lower BOLD responses to faces than objects are typically observed (Pelphrey et al., 2003; Kanwisher, 2017; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanwisher et al., 1997.

claim: Microelectrodes in P2 fell in the medial MidFG portion (FG3).
source: While microelectrodes recording single-unit activity located in the lateral portion of P1's middle fusiform gyrus (MidFG) (i.e., in cytoarchitectonic area FG4; Lorenz et al., 2017), a region known to elicit larger BOLD activity to faces than non-face objects ('Fusiform Face Area', FFA; Kanwisher et al., 1997), in P2 they fell in the medial MidFG portion (FG3), in which lower BOLD responses to faces than objects are typically observed (Pelphrey et al., 2003; Kanwisher, 2017; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of electrode location in P2.

claim: The medial MidFG portion (FG3) typically shows lower BOLD responses to faces than objects.
source: While microelectrodes recording single-unit activity located in the lateral portion of P1's middle fusiform gyrus (MidFG) (i.e., in cytoarchitectonic area FG4; Lorenz et al., 2017), a region known to elicit larger BOLD activity to faces than non-face objects ('Fusiform Face Area', FFA; Kanwisher et al., 1997), in P2 they fell in the medial MidFG portion (FG3), in which lower BOLD responses to faces than objects are typically observed (Pelphrey et al., 2003; Kanwisher, 2017; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pelphrey et al., 2003; Kanwisher, 2017; Gao et al., 2018.

claim: Robust differential activity to natural images of faces vs. non-face categories was objectively recorded with a frequency-tagging paradigm in fMRI in both MidFG regions sampled.
source: In both MidFG regions sampled, robust differential activity to natural images of faces vs. non-face categories was objectively recorded with a similar well-validated frequency-tagging paradigm in fMRI (Figure 1A) and microelectrode electrophysiological recordings (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Robust differential activity to natural images of faces vs. non-face categories was objectively recorded with a frequency-tagging paradigm in microelectrode electrophysiological recordings in both MidFG regions sampled.
source: In both MidFG regions sampled, robust differential activity to natural images of faces vs. non-face categories was objectively recorded with a similar well-validated frequency-tagging paradigm in fMRI (Figure 1A) and microelectrode electrophysiological recordings (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Faces elicited larger BOLD responses than non-face objects in the lateral MidFG.
source: As expected, faces elicited larger BOLD responses than non-face objects in the lateral MidFG, but lower responses in the medial MidFG (Pelphrey et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Experimental finding supported by citations to Pelphrey et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2018.

claim: Faces elicited lower BOLD responses than non-face objects in the medial MidFG.
source: As expected, faces elicited larger BOLD responses than non-face objects in the lateral MidFG, but lower responses in the medial MidFG (Pelphrey et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Experimental finding supported by citations to Pelphrey et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2018.

claim: Microwires in P1 (estimated Talairach location −40, –46, –19) fell in the lateral MidFG face-selective region: the Fusiform Face Area ('FFA', peak coordinate: −35, –51, –18).
source: Microwires in P1 (estimated Talairach location −40, –46, –19; Figure 2A) fell in the lateral MidFG face-selective region: the Fusiform Face Area ('FFA', peak coordinate: −35, –51, –18; Quian Quiroga et al., 2023), while microwires in P2 (29, −41, −12; Figure 2D) were located in the medial MidFG, an unprecedented sampled region with lower (deactivated) BOLD signal for faces.
evidence: Anatomical localization data with citation to Quian Quiroga et al., 2023 and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Microwires in P2 (29, −41, −12) were located in the medial MidFG, an unprecedented sampled region with lower (deactivated) BOLD signal for faces.
source: Microwires in P1 (estimated Talairach location −40, –46, –19; Figure 2A) fell in the lateral MidFG face-selective region: the Fusiform Face Area ('FFA', peak coordinate: −35, –51, –18; Quian Quiroga et al., 2023), while microwires in P2 (29, −41, −12; Figure 2D) were located in the medial MidFG, an unprecedented sampled region with lower (deactivated) BOLD signal for faces.
evidence: Anatomical localization data with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Recordings of category-selective spiking activity in P1 and P2 took place over up to 11 days.
source: Recordings of category-selective spiking activity in P1 and P2 took place over up to 11 days, with single units detected on 7 microwires per session.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: Single units were detected on 7 microwires per session.
source: Recordings of category-selective spiking activity in P1 and P2 took place over up to 11 days, with single units detected on 7 microwires per session.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: Across all independent sessions, 245 units were recorded (N = 206 single-units, SU and N = 39 multi-units, MU; pooled over 4 sessions for P1 and 7 sessions for P2).
source: Across all independent sessions (i.e., on different half-days), we recorded 245 units (N = 206 single-units, SU and N = 39 multi-units, MU; pooled over 4 sessions for P1 and 7 sessions for P2) firing to variable pictures of faces and objects.
evidence: Quantitative experimental data.

claim: Only a small proportion of single neurons failed to respond (i.e., no significant base rate response: N = 10/62, 16.1% in P1; N = 17/144 11.8% in P2).
source: Despite a brief recording time for each unit (2 sequences of 70 s), only a small proportion of single neurons failed to respond (i.e., no significant base rate response: N = 10/62, 16.1% in P1; N = 17/144 11.8% in P2; all Z < 1.64, all ps < 0.05; and no difference between participants, p = 0.54, Pearson's χ²).
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference between participants in the proportion of neurons that failed to respond (p = 0.54, Pearson's χ²).
source: Despite a brief recording time for each unit (2 sequences of 70 s), only a small proportion of single neurons failed to respond (i.e., no significant base rate response: N = 10/62, 16.1% in P1; N = 17/144 11.8% in P2; all Z < 1.64, all ps < 0.05; and no difference between participants, p = 0.54, Pearson's χ²).
evidence: Statistical comparison between participants.

claim: A very high proportion of face-selective neurons (p < 0.05) was found in both activated and deactivated MidFG regions (P1: 98.1%; N = 51/52; P2: 86.6%; N = 110/127).
source: Among all visually responsive neurons, we found a very high proportion of face-selective neurons (p < 0.05) in both activated and deactivated MidFG regions (P1: 98.1%; N = 51/52; P2: 86.6%; N = 110/127).
evidence: Quantitative experimental data.

claim: At a more conservative threshold (p < 0.01), strong face-selectivity is observed (P1: 86.5%; N = 45/52; P2: 77.9%; N = 99/127).
source: Even at a more conservative threshold (p < 0.01), strong face-selectivity is observed (P1: 86.5%; N = 45/52; P2: 77.9%; N = 99/127; no difference between the two individuals, p = 0.27, Pearson's χ² test).
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference between the two individuals in face-selectivity at the p < 0.01 threshold (p = 0.27, Pearson's χ² test).
source: Even at a more conservative threshold (p < 0.01), strong face-selectivity is observed (P1: 86.5%; N = 45/52; P2: 77.9%; N = 99/127; no difference between the two individuals, p = 0.27, Pearson's χ² test).
evidence: Statistical comparison between individuals.

claim: The vast majority of face-selective neurons in the lateral MidFG (P1) showed a significant relative increase in spike rate to faces (88.9% increases [N = 40/45] vs 11.1% decreases [N = 5/45]).
source: While the vast majority of face-selective neurons in the lateral MidFG (P1) showed a significant relative increase in spike rate to faces (88.9% increases [N = 40/45] vs 11.1% decreases [N = 5/45]; Figure 2B and C), most neurons in the medial MidFG (P2) showed significant relative spike rate decrease to faces (95.9% decreases [N = 95/99] vs 4.1% increases [N = 4/99]; Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with reference to Figure 2B and C.

claim: Most neurons in the medial MidFG (P2) showed significant relative spike rate decrease to faces (95.9% decreases [N = 95/99] vs 4.1% increases [N = 4/99]).
source: While the vast majority of face-selective neurons in the lateral MidFG (P1) showed a significant relative increase in spike rate to faces (88.9% increases [N = 40/45] vs 11.1% decreases [N = 5/45]; Figure 2B and C), most neurons in the medial MidFG (P2) showed significant relative spike rate decrease to faces (95.9% decreases [N = 95/99] vs 4.1% increases [N = 4/99]; Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with reference to Figure 2E and F.

claim: The mean onset response latency did not differ between increases and decreases (118.2 ms vs. 127.3 ms, respectively; p > 0.05, two-tailed percentile bootstrap).
source: While the mean onset response latency did not differ between increases and decreases (118.2 ms vs. 127.3 ms, respectively; p > 0.05, two-tailed percentile bootstrap; Figure 2C and F), a significantly lower response (i.e., absolute average firing rate) was found for decreases than increases ([130–300 ms]; 3.69 spikes/s for increases, ranging from 0.99 to 7.42 spikes/s; –2.73 spikes/s for decreases, ranging from –0.44 to –9.67 spikes/s; t-test p < 0.01).
evidence: Statistical comparison of latencies with reference to Figure 2C and F.

claim: A significantly lower response (i.e., absolute average firing rate) was found for decreases than increases ([130–300 ms]; 3.69 spikes/s for increases, ranging from 0.99 to 7.42 spikes/s; –2.73 spikes/s for decreases, ranging from –0.44 to –9.67 spikes/s; t-test p < 0.01).
source: While the mean onset response latency did not differ between increases and decreases (118.2 ms vs. 127.3 ms, respectively; p > 0.05, two-tailed percentile bootstrap; Figure 2C and F), a significantly lower response (i.e., absolute average firing rate) was found for decreases than increases ([130–300 ms]; 3.69 spikes/s for increases, ranging from 0.99 to 7.42 spikes/s; –2.73 spikes/s for decreases, ranging from –0.44 to –9.67 spikes/s; t-test p < 0.01).
evidence: Statistical comparison of firing rates.

claim: Among the 95 single units showing a reduced firing rate to faces (P2), 34 lacked a significant general visual response (at 6 Hz +12 Hz; i.e., 34.3%).
source: A final noteworthy observation is that, among the 95 single units showing a reduced firing rate to faces (P2), 34 lacked a significant general visual response (at 6 Hz +12 Hz; i.e., 34.3%; N = 21, 22.1% when only first 6 Hz harmonic considered, ps >0.01).
evidence: Quantitative experimental data.

claim: Responses of 'face-exclusive' single neurons reflect genuine suppression of baseline spiking activity upon presentation of a face.
source: Beyond a mere relative reduction to faces compared to non-face objects, responses of such 'face-exclusive' single neurons therefore appear to reflect genuine suppression of baseline spiking activity upon presentation of a face.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data based on the observation that some neurons lack general visual response but show face-selective decreases.

claim: BOLD signals correlate better with local field potentials (LFP) than spikes on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: Although BOLD signals correlate better with local field potentials (LFP) than spikes on a trial-by-trial basis (Logothetis et al., 2001), positive correlations have been observed between SU and BOLD in human (Mukamel et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007) and non-human primates (Goense and Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Logothetis et al., 2001.

claim: Positive correlations have been observed between SU and BOLD in human.
source: Although BOLD signals correlate better with local field potentials (LFP) than spikes on a trial-by-trial basis (Logothetis et al., 2001), positive correlations have been observed between SU and BOLD in human (Mukamel et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007) and non-human primates (Goense and Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mukamel et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007.

claim: Positive correlations have been observed between SU and BOLD in non-human primates.
source: Although BOLD signals correlate better with local field potentials (LFP) than spikes on a trial-by-trial basis (Logothetis et al., 2001), positive correlations have been observed between SU and BOLD in human (Mukamel et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007) and non-human primates (Goense and Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goense and Logothetis, 2008.

claim: There is a striking correspondence between increases/decreases in BOLD activity and (SU) neuronal firing, in two neighboring areas of the human association cortex.
source: Here, thanks to a unique combination of fMRI and microelectrode recordings in the same individual human brains, we report a striking correspondence between increases/decreases in BOLD activity and (SU) neuronal firing, in two neighboring areas of the human association cortex.
evidence: Summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: The sign of the BOLD signal fluctuation during visual stimulation matches the sign of SU activity.
source: By showing that the sign of the BOLD signal fluctuation during visual stimulation matches the sign of SU activity, our findings shed light on the physiology of BOLD signals, revealing in particular that BOLD decreases can be due to relative, or absolute (or a combination of both), spike suppression in the human brain.
evidence: Summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: BOLD decreases can be due to relative, or absolute (or a combination of both), spike suppression in the human brain.
source: By showing that the sign of the BOLD signal fluctuation during visual stimulation matches the sign of SU activity, our findings shed light on the physiology of BOLD signals, revealing in particular that BOLD decreases can be due to relative, or absolute (or a combination of both), spike suppression in the human brain.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: Transient spikes suppression could be due to suppression/reduction of synaptic inputs to the recorded neuron(s) or to inhibitory inputs to the neuron(s).
source: Such transient spikes suppression could be due to suppression/reduction of synaptic inputs to the recorded neuron(s) or to inhibitory inputs to the neuron(s).
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed spike suppression.

claim: The same contrasted pattern of BOLD activation/deactivation for faces in the lateral/medial portions of the fusiform gyrus has been systematically observed across hemispheres.
source: First, notwithstanding the right hemisphere's dominance in human face recognition (Jonas et al., 2016; Kanwisher, 2017; Gao et al., 2018), the same contrasted pattern of BOLD activation/deactivation for faces in the lateral/medial portions of the fusiform gyrus, respectively, has been systematically observed across hemispheres (Pelphrey et al., 2003; Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pelphrey et al., 2003 and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The right hemisphere shows dominance in human face recognition.
source: First, notwithstanding the right hemisphere's dominance in human face recognition (Jonas et al., 2016; Kanwisher, 2017; Gao et al., 2018), the same contrasted pattern of BOLD activation/deactivation for faces in the lateral/medial portions of the fusiform gyrus, respectively, has been systematically observed across hemispheres (Pelphrey et al., 2003; Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jonas et al., 2016; Kanwisher, 2017; Gao et al., 2018.

claim: The proportions of face-selective units did not differ between the two individuals tested.
source: Second, while a larger number of single units was found for P2 than P1 recordings, the proportions of face-selective units did not differ between the two individuals tested.
evidence: Statistical comparison between individuals.

claim: Neurons showing suppression of activity to faces have been reported in the monkey inferior temporal cortex.
source: Neurons showing suppression of activity to faces have been reported in the monkey inferior temporal cortex (Salehi et al., 2020), including inside face-selective cortical regions (Tsao et al., 2006; Bell et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Salehi et al., 2020; Tsao et al., 2006; Bell et al., 2011.

claim: There is a lack of reported BOLD deactivation to faces in the monkey brain.
source: However, both the lack of reported BOLD deactivation to faces in the monkey brain and of a fusiform gyrus in non-hominoid primates Weiner and Zilles, 2016 have prevented single-unit recordings in macaque monkeys to address this issue.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in monkey research.

claim: Non-hominoid primates lack a fusiform gyrus.
source: However, both the lack of reported BOLD deactivation to faces in the monkey brain and of a fusiform gyrus in non-hominoid primates Weiner and Zilles, 2016 have prevented single-unit recordings in macaque monkeys to address this issue.
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiner and Zilles, 2016.

claim: Faces elicit a strong decrease of neuronal activity relative to non-face objects in the medial MidFG.
source: Here, our neurophysiological recordings in humans suggest that faces do not only elicit a strong decrease of neuronal activity relative to non-face objects in the medial MidFG, but a genuine suppression of baseline spiking activity in a substantial proportion of the units recorded.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings.

claim: Faces elicit a genuine suppression of baseline spiking activity in a substantial proportion of the units recorded in the medial MidFG.
source: Here, our neurophysiological recordings in humans suggest that faces do not only elicit a strong decrease of neuronal activity relative to non-face objects in the medial MidFG, but a genuine suppression of baseline spiking activity in a substantial proportion of the units recorded.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings.

claim: Face-selective neural activity in the human brain can be expressed both as increase and active suppression of spiking activity.
source: Thus, beyond contributing to clarifying the physiological basis of the fMRI signal, our study sheds light on the nature of face-selective neural activity in the human brain, which can be expressed both as increase and active suppression of spiking activity.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings and their interpretation.

claim: Inhibitory cellular activity is thought to play an important balancing role in maintaining stable function of cortical circuits.
source: Inhibitory cellular activity is thought to play an important balancing role in maintaining stable function of cortical circuits (Vogels et al., 2011) and has been shown to play a key role in cortical category selectivity (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vogels et al., 2011.

claim: Inhibitory cellular activity has been shown to play a key role in cortical category selectivity.
source: Inhibitory cellular activity is thought to play an important balancing role in maintaining stable function of cortical circuits (Vogels et al., 2011) and has been shown to play a key role in cortical category selectivity (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2000.

claim: The study included two right-handed participants (two males, aged 23 and 46) who were patients undergoing clinical intracerebral evaluation with depth electrodes (SEEG) for refractory partial epilepsy.
source: The study included two right-handed participants (two males, aged 23 and 46) who were patients undergoing clinical intracerebral evaluation with depth electrodes (SEEG; Talairach and Bencaud, 1973) for refractory partial epilepsy in the Epilepsy Unit of the University Hospital of Nancy, France, in 2019 (P1) and 2023 (P2).
evidence: Description of study participants.

claim: The participants gave written informed consent to participate in the study (REUNIE, 2015-A01951-48).
source: The participants gave written informed consent to participate in the study (REUNIE, 2015-A01951-48), which was approved by a national ethical committee (CPP Est III, N°16.02.01).
evidence: Statement about ethical approval and consent.

claim: The study was approved by a national ethical committee (CPP Est III, N°16.02.01).
source: The participants gave written informed consent to participate in the study (REUNIE, 2015-A01951-48), which was approved by a national ethical committee (CPP Est III, N°16.02.01).
evidence: Statement about ethical approval.

claim: Electrophysiological data were recorded from Behnke-Fried hybrid micro-macro electrodes (Ad-Tech Medical Instrument).
source: Electrophysiological data were recorded from Behnke-Fried hybrid micro-macro electrodes (Ad-Tech Medical Instrument).
evidence: Description of recording equipment.

claim: Electrode implantation sites were determined based on non-invasive data collected during the early stages of the investigation and were verified by CT scan fused with a pre-operative T1-weighted MRI.
source: Electrode implantation sites were determined based on non-invasive data collected during the early stages of the investigation and were verified by CT scan fused with a pre-operative T1-weighted MRI.
evidence: Description of electrode localization procedure.

claim: The macro-microelectrodes are electrodes with macro-contacts modified to include 8 recording microwires and one reference, protruding about 3–4 mm beyond the tip of the macro-electrode.
source: The present report focuses on recordings from the macro-microelectrodes, i.e., electrodes with macro-contacts modified to include 8 recording microwires and one reference, protruding about 3–4 mm beyond the tip of the macro-electrode (Ad-Tech Medical; see Salado et al., 2018 for details about the macroelectrode implantation procedure).
evidence: Description of electrode design with citation to Salado et al., 2018.

claim: The microwires' signals were recorded at a 30 kHz sampling rate, using a 256-channel amplifier (BlackRock Microsystems), and recording activity was band-pass filtered (0.3–7500 Hz).
source: The microwires' signals were recorded at a 30 kHz sampling rate, using a 256-channel amplifier (BlackRock Microsystems), and recording activity was band-pass filtered (0.3–7500 Hz).
evidence: Description of recording parameters.

claim: Microelectrode data were recorded during 3 days (8 sequences performed in P1) and 11 days (14 sequences performed in P2).
source: Here, we report microelectrode data recorded during 3 days (8 sequences performed in P1) and 11 days (14 sequences performed in P2).
evidence: Description of data collection timeline.

claim: Participants were tested individually and seated at 80 cm from the computer screen.
source: Participants were tested individually and seated at 80 cm from the computer screen.
evidence: Description of experimental setup.

claim: The exact position of each contact from the micro-macro electrode relative to the individual brain anatomy was determined by coregistrating the post-operative CT scan with a T1-weighted MRI of the patient.
source: The exact position of each contact from the micro-macro electrode relative to the individual brain anatomy was determined in each participant's brain by coregistrating the post-operative CT scan with a T1-weighted MRI of the patient.
evidence: Description of localization procedure.

claim: The microwires' coordinates were estimated at approximately 4 mm from the tip of the macroelectrode.
source: The microwires' coordinates were estimated at approximately 4 mm from the tip of the macroelectrode.
evidence: Description of coordinate estimation method.

claim: All participants performed an fMRI face localizer a few months after the SEEG procedure, using an fMRI version of the frequency-tagging paradigm.
source: In addition, the location of microwires relative to fMRI-defined face-selective regions was determined by having all participants perform an fMRI face localizer a few months after the SEEG procedure, using an fMRI version of the frequency-tagging paradigm providing high SNR and reliability (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of experimental procedure with citation to Gao et al., 2018.

claim: Stimuli were selected from a large pool of 200 to 218 non-face object images and 45 to 48 face images.
source: Stimuli were selected from a large pool of 200 to 218 non-face object images and 45 to 48 face images (as in e.g., Jonas et al., 2016), presented in grayscale or color sequences.
evidence: Description of stimulus set with citation to Jonas et al., 2016.

claim: Images were equalized for mean pixel luminance and contrast.
source: Images were equalized for mean pixel luminance and contrast, but low-level visual cues associated with the two categories (faces and objects) remained highly variable, naturally minimizing the contribution of low-level visual cues to the face-selective neural responses (Rossion et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of stimulus preparation with citation to Rossion et al., 2015.

claim: Low-level visual cues associated with the two categories (faces and objects) remained highly variable, naturally minimizing the contribution of low-level visual cues to the face-selective neural responses.
source: Images were equalized for mean pixel luminance and contrast, but low-level visual cues associated with the two categories (faces and objects) remained highly variable, naturally minimizing the contribution of low-level visual cues to the face-selective neural responses (Rossion et al., 2015).
evidence: Explanation of stimulus design rationale with citation to Rossion et al., 2015.

claim: In the fMRI version, mini-face blocks ('bursts') were presented for 2.167 s every 9 s to account for the sluggishness of the BOLD response.
source: In the fMRI version (from Gao et al., 2018; also, Laurent et al., 2023), mini-face blocks ('bursts') were presented for 2.167 s every 9 s to account for the sluggishness of the BOLD response (i.e., F = 1/9 = 0.111 Hz).
evidence: Description of fMRI paradigm design with citations to Gao et al., 2018 and Laurent et al., 2023.

claim: Each fMRI sequence lasted 405 s and contained 44 cycles of face bursts.
source: Each fMRI sequence lasted 405 s and contained 44 cycles of face bursts (including a 4.5 s baseline at both the beginning and end of each sequence, respectively).
evidence: Description of fMRI sequence parameters.

claim: During intracerebral recordings, highly variable natural images of faces were inserted periodically every fifth image (i.e., face-selective frequency at 1.2 Hz = 6/5 Hz).
source: During intracerebral recordings, highly variable natural images of faces were inserted periodically every fifth image (i.e., face-selective frequency at 1.2 Hz = 6/5 Hz) as usually performed (Figure 1B; Rossion et al., 2015; Jonas et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of intracerebral recording paradigm with citations to Rossion et al., 2015 and Jonas et al., 2016, and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: A stimulation sequence lasted 70 s, including 66 s of stimulation at full contrast flanked by 2 s of fade-in and fade-out.
source: A stimulation sequence lasted 70 s, including 66 s of stimulation at full contrast flanked by 2 s of fade-in and fade-out, with gradual increases and decreases in contrast, respectively.
evidence: Description of stimulation sequence parameters.

claim: All images were presented with a sinusoidal stimulation contrast to provide a smooth transition between successive images.
source: All images were presented with a sinusoidal stimulation contrast to provide a smooth transition between successive images.
evidence: Description of stimulus presentation method.

claim: Participants were unaware of the periodicity of the faces.
source: Participants were unaware of the periodicity of the faces.
evidence: Description of participant awareness during experiment.

claim: During both fMRI and intracerebral recordings, participants stared at a small black cross presented at the center of the stimuli and detected rare brief nonperiodic color changes of the fixation cross.
source: During both fMRI and intracerebral recordings, participants stared at a small black cross presented at the center of the stimuli and detected rare brief nonperiodic color changes (70–10 times per sequence for fMRI/iEEG respectively, for 500 ms) of the fixation cross (black to red).
evidence: Description of task performed by participants.

claim: Spike detection and sorting/clustering were carried out using an automatic algorithm, based on a Bayesian approach.
source: Spike detection and sorting/clustering were carried out using an automatic algorithm, based on a Bayesian approach (Le Cam et al., 2023).
evidence: Description of spike sorting method with citation to Le Cam et al., 2023.

claim: The sorted clusters were visually reviewed and classified into single-units (SU) or multi-units (MU) based on their spike shape, variance, inter-spike interval distribution, and the presence of a refractory period.
source: The sorted clusters were visually reviewed and classified into single-units (SU) or multi-units (MU) based on their spike shape, variance, inter-spike interval distribution, and the presence of a refractory period.
evidence: Description of unit classification criteria.

claim: In all the sessions held by the two participants, 299 SU and 62 MU were identified.
source: In all the sessions held by the two participants, 299 SU and 62 MU were identified.
evidence: Quantitative data on identified units.

claim: An average of 2 units per contact was isolated.
source: An average of 2 units per contact was isolated.
evidence: Quantitative data on unit isolation.

claim: A discrete Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) was applied to the spike trains.
source: A discrete Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) was applied to the spike trains, and the resulting amplitude spectrum was cut into 1 Hz segments centered on the face-selective frequency and its three additional harmonics (i.e., 1.2 Hz, 2.4 Hz, 3.6 Hz, and 4.8 Hz), as well as on the base stimulation frequency and its harmonics (i.e., 6 Hz and 12 Hz).
evidence: Description of frequency-domain analysis method.

claim: A cluster (SU or MU) was considered as showing a significant response for faces and classified as 'face-selective' if the Z-score at the target frequency bin exceeded 1.64 (i.e., p < 0.05 one-tailed).
source: A cluster (SU or MU) was considered as showing a significant response for faces and classified as 'face-selective' if the Z-score at the target frequency bin exceeded 1.64 (i.e., p < 0.05 one-tailed).
evidence: Description of statistical criterion for face-selectivity.

claim: The face onset time was shifted forward by 33 ms (~1/5 of a 6 Hz cycle duration) to account for the sinusoidal modulation of contrast.
source: To account for the sinusoidal modulation of contrast, the face onset time was shifted forward by 33 ms (~1/5 of a 6 Hz cycle duration).
evidence: Description of temporal correction applied to data.

claim: The onset of face-selective response was delayed by 30–35 ms for sinusoidal visual stimulation compared to squarewave stimulation.
source: This delay was estimated by comparing SEEG responses to sequences presented with sinewave or squarewave (i.e., abrupt) contrast modulation of visual stimulation. The onset of face-selective response was delayed by 30–35 ms for sinusoidal visual stimulation, which corresponds to 4 screen refresh frames (33 ms) and 35% of the full contrast.
evidence: Experimental comparison to estimate temporal delay.

claim: The latency was computed as the time point at which net firing crossed the baseline +/-2.58 s.d. value (i.e., p < 0.01, two-tailed percentile bootstrap) for at least 30 ms.
source: Finally, the latency was computed as the time point at which net firing crossed the baseline +/-2.58 s.d. value (i.e., p < 0.01, two-tailed percentile bootstrap) for at least 30 ms, as described in Jacques et al., 2022.
evidence: Description of latency computation method with citation to Jacques et al., 2022.

claim: The two participants were scanned at the CHRU-Nancy, with a 3T Siemens Magnetom Prisma system with a 64-channel head-neck coil.
source: The two participants were scanned at the CHRU-Nancy, with a 3T Siemens Magnetom Prisma system (Siemens Medical System, Erlangen, Germany) with a 64-channel head-neck coil.
evidence: Description of fMRI scanning equipment.

claim: Anatomical images were collected using a high-resolution T1-weighted magnetization-prepared gradient-echo image (MP-RAGE) sequence.
source: Anatomical images were collected using a high-resolution T1-weighted magnetization-prepared gradient-echo image (MP-RAGE) sequence (192 sagittal slices, TR = 2300 ms, TE = 2.6 ms; flip angle (FA)=9°, field of view (FOV) = 256 × 256).
evidence: Description of anatomical imaging parameters.

claim: Functional images were collected with a T2*-weighted simultaneous multi-slice echo planar imaging (SMS EPI) sequence.
source: Functional images were collected with a T2*-weighted simultaneous multi-slice echo planar imaging (SMS EPI) sequence (TR = 1500 ms, TE = 30 ms, FA = 72°, FOV = 240 × 240 mm2, voxel size = 2.5 mm isotropic, matrix size = 96 × 96 for sequences done in 2019 or matrix size = 80 × 80 for sequences done in 2022, interleaved), which acquired 44 oblique-axial slices covering the entire temporal and occipital lobes.
evidence: Description of functional imaging parameters.

claim: The total duration of each sequence (run) for P1 (tested in 2019) was 333 s, including 9 s of dummy scans (222 TRs).
source: The total duration of each sequence (run) for P1 (tested in 2019) was 333 s, including 9 s of dummy scans (222 TRs).
evidence: Description of fMRI sequence duration for P1.

claim: The total duration of each run for P2 (tested in 2022) was 405 s including 9 s of dummy scans (270 TRs).
source: The total duration of each run for P2 (tested in 2022) was 405 s including 9 s of dummy scans (270 TRs).
evidence: Description of fMRI sequence duration for P2.

claim: The images subtended a viewing angle of 8° × 8° (33.4 cm × 33.4 cm) at a viewing distance of 240 cm.
source: The images subtended a viewing angle of 8° × 8° (33.4 cm × 33.4 cm) at a viewing distance of 240 cm.
evidence: Description of visual stimulus parameters during fMRI.

claim: Three fMRI sequences were performed for each patient, who was scanned 6–8 weeks after the microelectrode recordings.
source: Three fMRI sequences were performed for each patient, who was scanned 6–8 weeks after the microelectrode recordings.
evidence: Description of fMRI data collection timeline.

claim: The volumes of each run were first rigidly realigned with each other, and a mean functional image of the runs was computed for co-registration with the anatomical image, using SPM12.
source: As in Laurent et al., 2023, the volumes of each run were first rigidly realigned with each other, and a mean functional image of the runs was computed for co-registration with the anatomical image, using SPM12.
evidence: Description of fMRI preprocessing with citation to Laurent et al., 2023.

claim: The volumes were spatially smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 2 mm (FWHM).
source: The volumes were also spatially smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 2 mm (FWHM; i.e., full width at half maximum).
evidence: Description of fMRI preprocessing step.

claim: A Fourier analysis was performed using the FFT function in MATLAB without windowing.
source: Then, a Fourier analysis was performed using the FFT function in MATLAB without windowing.
evidence: Description of fMRI analysis method.

claim: Amplitudes at the face stimulation frequency (i.e., at F = 0.111 Hz) were converted into Z-scores, using the mean and standard deviation of the amplitude at neighboring frequencies.
source: Amplitudes at the face stimulation frequency (i.e., at F = 0.111 Hz) were converted into Z-scores, using the mean and standard deviation of the amplitude at neighboring frequencies (see Gao et al., 2018 for details).
evidence: Description of fMRI analysis method with citation to Gao et al., 2018.

claim: The relative activations and deactivations of the neural responses at the face stimulation frequency were defined by the phase of the BOLD response.
source: The relative activations and deactivations of the neural responses at the face stimulation frequency were defined by the phase of the BOLD response.
evidence: Description of method for determining activation vs. deactivation.

claim: About 70% of neurons were face-selective in both individual brains tested across multiple recording sessions.
source: In both individual brains tested across multiple recording sessions, a frequency-tagging stimulation objectively identified a substantial proportion (about 70%) of face-selective neurons.
evidence: Quantitative summary of face-selectivity findings from the abstract.

claim: Single units recorded in the lateral FG showed a selective increase to faces.
source: While single units recorded in the lateral FG showed a selective increase to faces, neurons localized in the medial FG decreased spiking activity selectively to faces.
evidence: Summary of main experimental finding from the abstract.

claim: Neurons localized in the medial FG decreased spiking activity selectively to faces.
source: While single units recorded in the lateral FG showed a selective increase to faces, neurons localized in the medial FG decreased spiking activity selectively to faces.
evidence: Summary of main experimental finding from the abstract.

claim: About a third of the single neurons found in the medial FG showed genuine suppression of baseline spiking activity upon presentation of a face.
source: Beyond a relative reduction to faces compared to non-face objects, about a third of the single neurons found in the medial FG showed genuine suppression of baseline spiking activity upon presentation of a face.
evidence: Quantitative summary of suppression findings from the abstract.

claim: The frequency-tagging paradigm provides robust population-level face-selective activity devoid of low-level sensory confounds at the tagged frequencies.
source: With both recording methods (and EEG; Rossion et al., 2015), this paradigm provides robust population-level face-selective activity devoid of low-level sensory confounds at the tagged frequencies.
evidence: Statement about the properties of the paradigm with citation to Rossion et al., 2015 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of the BOLD response time courses is used to define face-selective voxels in the frequency domain (0.111 Hz).
source: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of the BOLD response time courses is used to define face-selective voxels in the frequency domain (0.111 Hz; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of fMRI analysis method with citation to Gao et al., 2018.

claim: BOLD frequency spectra at each voxel are transformed into Z-scores, which can either be positive (higher response to face than non-face stimuli, i.e., BOLD signal increase) or negative (lower response to faces than non-face stimuli, i.e., BOLD signal decrease).
source: BOLD frequency spectra at each voxel are transformed into Z-scores, which can either be positive (higher response to face than non-face stimuli, i.e., BOLD signal increase) or negative (lower response to faces than non-face stimuli, i.e., BOLD signal decrease).
evidence: Description of how BOLD activation and deactivation are defined.

claim: The estimated location of the microelectrode falls in left MidFG activation in P1.
source: The estimated location of the microelectrode (green circle) falls in left MidFG activation in P1 and right MidFG deactivation in P2.
evidence: Description of electrode location relative to fMRI activation, with reference to Figure 2A and D.

claim: The estimated location of the microelectrode falls in right MidFG deactivation in P2.
source: The estimated location of the microelectrode (green circle) falls in left MidFG activation in P1 and right MidFG deactivation in P2.
evidence: Description of electrode location relative to fMRI deactivation, with reference to Figure 2A and D.

claim: The representative face-selective SU in P2 exhibits a high increase in firing rate to the general visual stimulation at 6 Hz.
source: The representative face-selective SU in panel E also exhibits a high increase in firing rate to the general visual stimulation at 6 Hz.
evidence: Description of a specific neuron's response pattern with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: The average time courses are computed on notch-filtered data to remove the general visual response at 6 Hz and harmonics.
source: Note that the average time courses are computed on notch-filtered data to remove the general visual response at 6 Hz and harmonics (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Description of data processing method with reference to Figure 2C and F.
